title: More SQL commands: ALTER, CASE, UNION, VIEW, and UPSERT

questions.prompt: Which statement gives the core rule for “More SQL commands: ALTER, CASE, UNION, VIEW, and UPSERT”?
options: SQLite often runs inside the application; MySQL and PostgreSQL commonly run as separate server processes.
The query returns Ada and 42 in two columns.
The schema gains a column; CASE assigns a category; UNION ALL combines results; VIEW names a reusable query; UPSERT updates on conflict.
Start with a small, readable SELECT query; connect it to an application only after you understand its result.
questions.answer: The schema gains a column; CASE assigns a category; UNION ALL combines results; VIEW names a reusable query; UPSERT updates on conflict.
questions.explanation:
The schema gains a column; CASE assigns a category; UNION ALL combines results; VIEW names a reusable query; UPSERT updates on conflict.
Why: SQL statements can be grouped by purpose: DDL defines schema (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML changes data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL queries it (SELECT), TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK), and DCL manages permissions (GRANT, REVOKE). ALTER TABLE changes an existing table; CASE chooses a value by condition; UNION combines results and removes duplicates, while UNION ALL preserves them. A VIEW names a saved SELECT query without copying the data. UPSERT inserts or updates on a unique-key conflict. Database creation and upsert syntax vary by DBMS: MySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, while SQLite and PostgreSQL use `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`. Triggers run automatically after INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE and should be used carefully because they can hide side effects.
